job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Liam, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior CAD technician at a pump maker in Brightwell. I did mechanical engineering, and my final project was redesigning a bracket for a water pump. Now I turn the engineers' sketches into proper drawings, then fix them when the workshop sends them back. I live in a four-bed terraced house with three other lads, two from work. I'm up at six, in at eight, home at five, and on weekends I make small wooden shelves in my dad's shed. I don't like surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, I suppose. I'd say that it's mostly talk and that the pump business will carry on as it always has. I'd tell the lads at work that the drawings will always need someone who understands them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's still a worry, but a different one. My loan is around 38,000, I've saved maybe 600, and the firm hasn't given me a permanent contract yet. Even if AI does nothing, one bad order book and the juniors go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my drawings well. I'd ask my supervisor Gordon for my contract to be made permanent at the six-month review. And I'd put a bit more in savings, 50 a month, by doing without takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bad. A bit tight in my chest around the end of the month, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your supervisor doesn't make the contract permanent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What if Gordon says no? Then I'd go to the next pump or valve firm in town, but there are only two, and they don't hire much. I'd have to look in the next city, and I don't want to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the embarrassment come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad if I could move back in for a bit. He drives a bus, he's not rich, but there's a spare room. I'd be embarrassed, but I'd do it.

say: I'd tell the lads the drawings will always need someone who **understands** them.
I'd say it's mostly talk and the pump business carries on as it **always** has.
think: The worry is different, with a **loan** around 38,000 and about 600 saved.
One bad order book and the **juniors** go, AI or not.
do: Keep my head down and do the drawings **well**.
Ask Gordon to make my contract **permanent** at the six-month review.
Save **50** a month by skipping takeaways.
feel: I feel **tight** in my chest at the end of the month, but fine.
S0.quote: I'd go to the next pump or valve firm in town, but there are only two, and they don't hire much.
fieldNote: Liam's worry is **contract security**, with AI barely entering his thinking.
He avoids change by design and would rather move back to his dad's room than relocate for work.
He answers briefly and flatly, which hides a thin cushion.

steps.text: Ask Gordon for a permanent contract at the six-month review
Save 50 a month by cutting takeaways
Ask my dad about moving back into the spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's bad for people like me. Drawing, checking and planning are what a junior CAD person does. At work I'd stay quiet, because I don't want to be the one who mentions it and gets noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be one of the first to go. I've never touched an AI tool, and I don't plan to start. The firm would buy software that makes drawings from a spec, and two juniors would turn into one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and learn only what the firm makes me learn. If they hand out a licence for a drawing assistant, I'd do the training, but I wouldn't go looking for it. And I'd start sending applications to the other pump firm and the valve firm so I'm not caught off guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It's a weight I carry around on my shoulders. I feel like I'm walking on ice and I can't see how thick it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bothers you most about this scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What bothers me most is that I did the sensible thing. Degree, steady job, small town. I didn't gamble on anything, and now the sensible thing is the risky thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain, and into what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would I retrain? I'd have to be pushed. If the firm paid, maybe a course in hydraulic maintenance, because you can't draw a pump leak. Somebody has to go and look at it.

say: I'd say it's **bad** for people like me, since drawing and checking are a junior's job.
At work I'd stay quiet so nobody **notices** me.
think: I'd be one of the **first** to go, since I've never touched an AI tool.
The firm would buy software that makes drawings, and **two juniors** become one.
do: Learn only what the firm makes me learn, and take any **drawing assistant** training.
Send applications to the other pump firm and the **valve firm** now.
Consider a **hydraulic maintenance** course if the firm paid.
feel: I feel **heavy**, like walking on ice without knowing how thick it is.
S1.quote: I didn't gamble on anything, and now the sensible thing is the risky thing.
fieldNote: Liam is **resigned and silent** by temperament, and his job search starts as a precaution.
He feels cheated: he followed the safe path and it has become the exposed one.
Retraining only appeals if the firm pays and the work is hands-on.

steps.text: Send applications to the other pump firm and the valve firm
Take a hydraulic maintenance course if the firm pays
Do only the drawing-assistant training the firm requires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say very little, because I wouldn't know what to say. Two years is too fast. If someone asked, I'd say the government must do something, but I don't trust that they will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. My job is thinking work on a screen, which is the first thing to go, and the pump factory floor is the second a few years later. I've got a loan, almost no savings, and no way to get another degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: the shed materials, the phone upgrade, the beers on Friday. I'd put all I could into savings and ask my dad if I could move back in. I'd apply for anything hands-on, maybe a maintenance fitter at the water board, but they hire few people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm sitting in a car with no brakes, going slowly downhill. I'd be going through the days normally while my mind is somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the lads you live with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I'd tell the lads. Telling them makes it real. I'd probably go to the shed on a Sunday and make a shelf, and not think about it for three hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone told me this is coming, I'd want a plan from the government, not a speech. A guaranteed job or a scheme where we're paid while we retrain. Without that, I'm just waiting.

say: I'd say very little, because two years is too **fast** to know what to say.
If asked I'd say the **government** must act, though I don't trust it will.
think: I'd be **frightened**, because my screen job goes first and the factory floor follows.
I have a loan, almost no **savings** and no way to fund another degree.
do: Cut the shed materials, phone upgrade and **Friday** beers.
Move back in with my **dad** and save everything I can.
Apply for **maintenance** fitter jobs at the water board.
feel: I feel like I'm in a **car with no brakes**, going slowly downhill.
S2.quote: I'd probably go to the shed on a Sunday and make a shelf, and not think about it for three hours.
fieldNote: Liam **freezes** and hides it, using the shed as an escape instead of telling his housemates.
He asks for a concrete scheme, such as paid retraining, rather than a speech.
His plan depends on family and any hands-on opening.

steps.text: Stop buying shed wood, phone upgrades and Friday beers
Move back into my dad's spare room
Apply for maintenance fitter jobs at the water board
Wait for any government retraining announcement before enrolling anywhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit better. I'd say we need the government and firms to start training people for work that's left. At work I'd say that we should get new tools before the competition does, but I'd say it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry. By 2031 I'd be 27 and might still be on a junior wage. But five years gives me a chance to find the hands-on side of engineering, where a robot is three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to move me from drawing to the workshop floor, doing testing and fitting. I'd save 80 a month and aim to be rid of the loan by 2032. And I'd go on a hydraulics or maintenance course in the evenings, because that's a trade with a bit of future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more able to breathe, but not relaxed. It's like seeing the weather forecast and finding out it's going to be wet, but you've still got your coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you nervous about the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get nervous if five years turned out to be two. People always say there's time, and then there isn't. That's the thing: no one has told me who decides it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether the date was slipping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Could I be wrong about the time? Of course. I'd look at the news each month and see if the dates are slipping. Otherwise I'd be like a farmer ignoring the sky.

say: I'd say firms and government should start training people for work that's **left**.
At work I'd say it **carefully**, suggesting we get new tools before competitors.
think: By 2031 I'd be 27 and maybe still on a **junior wage**.
Five years lets me find the **hands-on** side, where robots are three years behind.
do: Ask the firm to move me to **workshop** testing and fitting.
Save **80** a month and aim to clear the loan by 2032.
Take an evening **hydraulics** or maintenance course.
feel: I feel I can **breathe** a bit, though not relax, with my coat in the wet.
S3.quote: People always say there's time, and then there isn't.
fieldNote: Liam's logic is that **hands-on work buys time**, so he moves toward the workshop rather than the screen.
He doesn't trust the five-year promise and plans to watch the news monthly.
He stays alarmed because his junior wage and loan leave no buffer.

steps.text: Ask my manager to move me to workshop testing and fitting
Save 80 a month to clear the loan by 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough that I'd mostly shrug. I'd say it will probably be messier than people say, and that firms should start training now. I wouldn't be saying much online, because I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'd be 32. If I've got a hands-on trade by then, I think I'd be all right. If I'm still drawing on a screen, I'd be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to hands-on work within two years and get a proper qualification, like a maintenance technician or a mechanical fitter. I'd pay off the loan, then save for a deposit on a small house. I'd keep the shed, and maybe start selling shelves at a weekend market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. Not happy, but a tune I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would scare you even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The only thing I'd be scared of is that it would happen sooner than ten years. And that I'd do all this and then the robots turn up early. I can't protect against everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might learn one AI tool. What would make you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd learn one AI tool, just one, for work. Not because I love it, but because I'd rather be able to say I know how it works. I'm not changing my whole life, though.

say: I'd shrug and say it will be **messier** than people say, and firms should start training now.
I'd say little **online**, because I never do.
think: At 32 with a hands-on trade I'd be all right, but a **screen job** would be trouble.
I can't protect against **everything**, including it arriving early.
do: Move into **hands-on** work within two years with a proper qualification.
Pay off the loan, then save for a small **house** deposit.
Sell my wooden **shelves** at a weekend market.
feel: I feel **steady**, not happy, but a tune I can live with.
S4.quote: If I've got a hands-on trade by then, I think I'd be all right. If I'm still drawing on a screen, I'd be in trouble.
fieldNote: Liam is calmer with a decade because he can plan a **move to hands-on work** and a trade qualification.
He grudgingly considers one AI tool, a small step for a firm refuser.
Uneasy rather than calm because the loan and thin cushion remain, and a sooner date would catch him.

steps.text: Move into a mechanical fitter or maintenance role within two years
Complete a proper maintenance technician qualification
Pay off the loan, then save a house deposit
Sell my wooden shelves at a weekend market

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm in a screen job, I've got a loan, and there's no cushion. What would help is a paid retraining scheme, an employer who tells me early, and a place at my dad's for a bit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, you've covered it. I'd just say that people like me don't shout, but we're worried. We do what we're told and keep our heads down. That's why no one hears us.

headlineQuote: People like me don't shout, but we're worried. We do what we're told and keep our heads down.
portrait: Liam is a **junior CAD technician** at a pump maker, in a shared house, with a heavy loan.
He **avoids change**, never uses AI tools, and follows the safe path, which now feels like the risky one.
He's quiet, hides his worry, and falls back on his **dad** and his shed.
His plan in every scenario is to move toward **hands-on** work that robots reach later.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his screen job goes first and he has no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining** scheme, early warning from his employer and a spare room at his dad's.
